comments.author: GMoromisato
comments.text:
Starship is, essentially, Space Shuttle done right: fully reusable booster without solid boosters (avoids Challenger disaster) and orbiter stacked on top instead of on the side (avoid Columbia disaster).
The original designs for the Space Shuttle had the booster (with wings!) return to the launch site, but the cost for two new crewed vehicles was too large, so they scaled it back to the compromised version.
Even more revolutionary, compared to Shuttle, Starship is built on an assembly line. They can build a booster ever 4 weeks and a ship every 2 weeks.
The future we were promised in the 1970s is about to become real.

stories.title_en: How did Woz write the Apple 1 BASIC before building the computer?

comments.author: femto
comments.text:
What Woz did was the default way of writing assembly language programs for owners of 8-bit computers (mostly hobbyists).  You didn't have money for a second machine, so you wrote your program on paper, you entered it then tested it in situ.  Mostly you got it right, as doing it on paper was slow and meant you had the opportunity to put lots of thought into it.  8-bit instruction sets were simple enough that you eventually learned the most common instructions by heart.  There was a point where I could mostly translate a Z80 program from assembly to machine code from (my) memory.
Maybe that is part of the nostalgia for the 8-bit days: the practice of "slow programming"?  It was relaxing, sort of like those "slow tv" shows.

comments.author: mrandish
comments.text:
I got my first computer in 1981, a 4K Radio Shack Color Computer for $500 (a huge purchase decision at the time). So I missed hand assembling for bare metal and Altair-type toggles.
However, there was an interesting period of a few years where assembler tools were either unavailable or fairly expensive, so it was common to use the computer's BASIC to write an assembly language monitor program. Such program listings were pretty common in early hobbyist 'zines. It was also pretty common to use BASIC to POKE in a quick bootstrap program to load a value in a register and jump to an address, which I could usually do from memory. After 40 years I still remember the 6809 RTS was $39 and NOP was $12, two very handy instructions to POKE a quick mod into a program.

Long-term, it can be hard to sustain, and maybe a bit unhealthy – it becomes a form of self-betrayal, where you repeatedly suppress genuine negative feelings about dealing with someone difficult. Also, in more extreme cases, the sort of people who are prone to creating drama and conflict pick up on the technique and make it into a battle of wills – who will break and give up first. stories.title_en: Let's Write a PostScript Interpreter

comments.author: tonyedgecombe
comments.text:
My retirement project is a PostScript interpreter. I've done about 260 of the 286 operators in the original Apple LaserWriter. I'm about half way through the last tricky bit, Type 1 fonts.
The internals are quite interesting, I always assumed the interpreter just processed the input as it arrives but it actually starts a PostScript program as soon as the printer boots and that controls the hardware and handling incoming jobs. A lot of this code is available through a console, ie:
userdict begin /start load == end
dumps the first program started by the printer.
I have an original LaserWriter which works through the console but doesn't print. Luckily someone has done the work to get the firmware running in MAME.
My interest in this came from working with a QMS distributor in the eighties. At the time I didn't really have a chance to delve that deep into the technology but I was always fascinated by it.

comments.author: fsflyer
comments.text:
This brings back memories.  In the very early 90s I took a graduate level graphics class and one assignment was to write ray tracer.  The professor allowed any programming language in the class, so I used a language that was suited to the assignment.  The results had to be printed out to turn in, and color printers were rare, so the assignment was in grey scale.
The postscript image operator in Postscript takes a procedure to return data and it was simple to encode the scene in that procedure.  The Postscript image operator scaled the image data between the 500 pixels that image was required to be and the 300 dpi printer resolution and did the grey scale mapping.
The postscript program fit on two pages with comments, many classmates had C or Pascal programs over 20 pages.
The 12 MHz 68000 in the LaserWriter was faster than the 8 MHz in the early Macintoshes or the 4.77 MHz 8086 in the PC clones, so it actually ran faster than many of the other student's ray tracers.

comments.author: glkindlmann
comments.text:
I tried to write (in C) a PostScript byte compiler for a grad school project.  It
is
a very appealing language to work with, with the simplicity of stack machine. And like with this post, I didn't get into the graphical elements that make PostScript useful.
Mainly I learned that Ghostscript is doing a lot to make its PostScript interpreter fast: with the non-graphical test programs I could think up, GhostScript was many times faster interpreting the program (even computationally intensive ones) than my runtime (called "egon") could execute the byte-compiled PostScript.  So it was a computation fail but still a pedagogy win.
I've always been meaning to learn more about how Ghostscript is engineered.

comments.author: a4isms
comments.text:
My very first professional gig in the mid-80s was on a classified ad-taking application for what were then called penny-savers, physical newspaper-like publications that were nearly 100% classifieds. Penny-savers would be distributed in boxes around urban centres and could be very profitable. Our app ran on MP/M, a multi-user CP/M variant. And when it was time to go to print, our code generated PS directly, there was no "printer driver" or abstraction of any kind.
We sold our customers
two
Apple LaserWriters each, because if one went down just before going to print they'd be screwed. We would print on both in parallel for speed, but could fall back to just one. And the printed ads? Somebody over in the print shop would cut them out in strips and then paste those strips up to be photographed for the printing press. We didn't have full end-to-end digital yet.
PS wasn't easy, but it was very grokkable.

I built Fursoy Slice-1, a 64-bit out-of-order superscalar RISC-V core (RV64IMAFDV + Zba/Zbb/Zicsr/Zifencei) in SystemVerilog, along with a minimal SoC (5-master crossbar, CLINT, PLIC, 16550 UART, and custom SBI v2.0 firmware).
At a high level, the core is 2-wide fetch/decode/rename/retire with a 128-entry ROB, 160-entry integer PRF, 8 branch checkpoints for single-cycle speculative RAT rollback, and separate Int/Mem/FP/Vec issue queues. On the memory side, it has a dual-port Sv39 DTLB (64-entry 4-way Tree-PLRU + 8-entry 2 MiB/1 GiB superpage CAM), ITLB, and a 16 KiB 8-bank non-blocking L1D. Instead of flushing dirty lines on every page-table walk, the hardware PTW snoops dirty L1D sets non-destructively so Linux page-table updates are visible directly, paired with store-queue drain on SFENCE.VMA.
In Verilator, it boots mainline Linux 6.6.50 and BusyBox userspace in ~89.8M cycles (~76.2M retired instructions, 2,255 page faults handled) while checking an 8-bucket single-owner CPI conservation invariant every cycle with 0 cycle leakage. Synthesizing the 8 main core logic blocks standalone with sv2v + Yosys + OpenSTA on Nangate 45nm (SRAMs/PRFs black-boxed, pre-P&R) meets 500 MHz acros
